title: Computers Find Thousands of Hidden Steps in Turning CO2 Into Fuel
summary:
Carbon dioxide, or CO2, is a gas released when we burn fuels. Scientists are looking for ways to turn it into useful things, such as the fuel and chemical methanol. Now researchers in India have used artificial intelligence to find thousands of chemical reactions that earlier models had missed.

The team works at the Indian Institute of Science, also called IISc. Their study was published in the journal Nature Communications.

One way to recycle CO2 is to make it react with hydrogen with help from a catalyst. A catalyst is a material that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up. In this study, the catalyst was copper. The process involves a huge number of tiny reaction steps, too many to study one by one with powerful computer simulations. So scientists usually focus on only a few steps they think matter most.

The IISc team started with 152 reactions. They then trained machine learning programs, a type of AI, to quickly estimate how hard other reactions would be. Their network grew to 9,389 reactions.

That made a big difference. The small network wrongly predicted that the main product would be formic acid, not methanol. The bigger network matched real experiments and predicted about 40 times more CO2 being converted.

The bigger network also revealed a surprise. Hydrogen could sometimes join the reaction as a whole molecule, instead of first splitting into separate atoms. "The idea that hydrogen can transfer as an intact molecule, without first splitting into atoms, runs against what most of us were taught," said Shivam Chaturvedi, a student on the team.

The researchers say this could help scientists design better catalysts and study other important industrial processes.
why_it_matters: Finding better ways to turn carbon dioxide into fuels and chemicals could help reduce waste gas, and the AI method could speed up research on other industrial processes.
